Details of the conversion:

Integer precision: Int8 through Int64 and UInt8 through UInt32 fit PHP’s 64-bit int. UInt64, Int128, and UInt128 values beyond PHP_INT_MAX become float, as PHP’s own integer overflow does, so they lose precision above 2^53.
Decimal: values come back as strings, such as "1.25" for Decimal(10, 2), so no precision is lost.
Time units: Datetime defaults to microseconds. Datetime(ms) and Datetime(ns) keep their unit inside Polars, and PHP’s DateTimeImmutable holds microseconds. A Duration comes back as an integer count of its unit: 1.5 seconds in Duration(ms) is 1500.
Time zones: a naive Datetime comes back in UTC. A zoned Datetime, such as Datetime(us, America/New_York), comes back in its zone.
Null and NaN: null is a missing value of any type. NaN is a float value, and isNull() is false for it.
Lists and structs: a List or Array value is a PHP list, and a Struct value is an associative array keyed by field name.

From PHP, each column gets one inferred type. Integers widen to floats, nulls fit any type, DateTimeInterface values become naive Datetime(us) on their wall-clock time (the zone is not kept; use dt()->replaceTimeZone() to attach one), lists become List, and associative arrays become Struct. Any other mix raises SchemaError; pass a schema to set types.

title: Types and values
Reading and writing
text:
read_* functions return a DataFrame. scan_* functions return a LazyFrame, so filters and column selections are pushed into the reader. DataFrame::write*() writes a file; LazyFrame::sink*() streams a query’s result to a file without collecting it in memory.
read_database($query, $pdo) reads a query’s result from any PDO connection. params binds placeholders through prepare() and execute(). schemaOverrides casts columns afterwards, which helps with drivers that return numbers or dates as strings: ['d' => 'Date'] parses ISO date text.
$df->writeDatabase('table', $pdo) inserts the rows in batches inside a transaction and returns the row count. ifTableExists is fail (the default), append, or replace. A new table gets portable column types: BIGINT, DOUBLE PRECISION, TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE, and TIMESTAMP (DATETIME(6) on MySQL). List and struct values are stored as JSON text. It is tested against SQLite, PostgreSQL 17, and MySQL 8.4.
A scan runs when the query is collected. collect(engine: 'streaming') processes a large file in batches and keeps less of it in memory; Performance measures the difference.
Parquet, IPC, and JSON support are Cargo features. An extension built without one raises a ComputeError from that format’s functions.

title: DataFrame and LazyFrame
text: DataFrame holds data in memory and runs each operation immediately. LazyFrame records operations and runs them, optimized, on collect(). Both have the same verbs; a DataFrame builds each verb on a lazy query and collects it, as py-polars does.

title: DataFrame and LazyFrame

text:
Joins
join() takes on, or leftOn and rightOn, and how: inner, left, right, full, semi, anti, or cross. suffix names clashing right-hand columns, coalesce merges key columns, nullsEqual lets null keys match, and maintainOrder (none, left, right, left_right, right_left) fixes the row order.
$sales = read_csv('sales.csv')->select('id', 'store', 'units')->head(6);
$stores = read_csv('stores.csv')->filter(col('store')->ne('S2'));

echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'left', maintainOrder: 'left'), "\n";
echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'anti'), "\n";
echo $stores->rename(['store' => 'shop'])->join($sales, leftOn: 'shop', rightOn: 'store', how: 'inner')->height(), " matched rows\n";

text:
Time series
groupByDynamic() groups rows into fixed time windows, and rolling() gives each row a window that ends at it. joinAsof() matches each row to the nearest earlier (or later, or nearest) row of another data frame, optionally within by groups and a tolerance. Durations are py-polars strings such as '1d', '2h30m', '1w', and '1mo'. Expressions add the rolling*By() family and ewmMean(). The functions date_range() and datetime_range() build calendars.
$daily = read_csv('sales.csv', tryParseDates: true)
    ->groupBy('date')->agg(col('units')->sum())
    ->sort('date');

// Weeks starting on Monday.
echo $daily->groupByDynamic('date', every: '1w')->agg(col('units')->sum()->alias('week_units'))->head(3), "\n";

// The seven days ending at each row.
echo $daily->withColumns(col('units')->rollingSumBy('date', '7d')->alias('last_7d'))->head(4), "\n";

// The list price in force on each day.
$prices = (new DataFrame(['from' => [new DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'), new DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-05')], 'list_price' => [5.0, 5.5]]))
    ->cast(['from' => 'Date']);
echo $daily->head(4)->joinAsof($prices, leftOn: 'date', rightOn: 'from');

title: Performance
text:
Polars memory is outside PHP’s memory manager, so memory_limit does not count it. PHP arrays built from a result do count.
rows(), toDicts(), and iterRows() build PHP arrays for every row, which can take far more memory than the data does in Polars. Calling rows() on each slice from iterSlices(10000) keeps PHP’s peak low.
Collecting rows into PHP costs time in proportion to the rows and columns returned. Datetime columns cost the most, because each value becomes a DateTimeImmutable object.
A PolarsTable gains the most when a pipeline reduces the data (summaries, filters, or joins followed by summaries) or chains several verbs before collecting.
Reading files with Phpolars\read_csv() or read_parquet() and wrapping the result with PolarsTable::fromPolars() avoids parsing the file in PHP.
A verb given a PHP closure converts a PolarsTable to a phibble DataFrame and back. Use expressions on large data, or phibble’s in-memory DataFrame for closure-heavy pipelines.
For a filtered scan of a large file, collect(engine: 'streaming') runs in batches and keeps less in memory.

title: Performance
text:
Memory on large files

scan_csv() applies filters in the reader with either engine, so rows that a filter rejects are not kept.
With the default engine, kept rows can cost more than their own size. A String column that keeps a few strings from a parsed batch holds the batch’s whole buffer. The streaming engine copies the kept strings into buffers of their own.
Polars maps the CSV file into memory, so a process’s resident set size also includes up to the file’s size in pages that the operating system can reclaim.
tests/memory.php checks that a filtered streaming scan holds much less than the file.
The sink*() methods stream a result to a file without collecting it.

title: Getting started
text:
phpolars runs on PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5, non-thread-safe (NTS) builds, on Linux and macOS. Install it with PIE, PHP’s extension installer:
pie install phpstats/phpolars
On Linux on x86_64 and arm64 with glibc 2.34 or later, PIE downloads a prebuilt binary. On other platforms, including macOS, it builds the extension from source, which needs a stable Rust toolchain and libclang and takes several minutes. PIE then enables the extension in php.ini. Under PHP-FPM, restart FPM afterwards so that its workers load the extension. Deployment covers servers, Laravel Forge, Laravel Herd, and manual installs.

use function Phpolars\{col, len, read_csv};

title: Getting started
text:
Lazy queries
A DataFrame runs each method immediately. A LazyFrame records operations and runs them when collect() is called. scan_csv() creates a lazy query. Polars optimizes the column selection and the filters before running it, so the reader converts only the columns that the query uses and drops filtered rows as it parses them. The reader still reads the whole file. Query a large CSV file lazily walks through a query plan.
$query = scan_csv('sales.csv')
    ->filter(col('units')->gt(5))
    ->groupBy('store')
    ->agg(col('units')->sum())
    ->sort('store');

echo $query->explain(), "\n\n";
echo $query->collect();

  AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
    [col("units").sum()] BY [col("store")]
    FROM
    Csv SCAN [sales.csv]

    SELECTION: col("units") > 5

title: Getting started
text:
Missing values
phpolars follows Polars: a missing value is null, aggregates such as sum() and mean() skip it, and null sorts first. phibble and phplyr follow R and dplyr instead. phibble and phplyr compares the two.

title: Query a large CSV file lazily
text:
Filter and aggregate a CSV file with a lazy query, so that Polars can push the column selection and the filter into the CSV reader.
Requires the phpolars extension (Getting started). Runnable scripts: lazy-csv.setup.php and lazy-csv.php.






NoteMake the input file





The setup script writes orders.csv, one million orders in six columns (53 MB), to the current directory. It stops if the file already exists.
use Phpolars\DataFrame;
use function Phpolars\{col, int_range};

if (file_exists('orders.csv')) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "orders.csv already exists.\n");
    exit(1);
}

$id = col('order_id');
(new DataFrame(['i' => [0]]))
    ->select(int_range(0, 1_000_000)->alias('order_id'))
    ->withColumns(
        $id->mod(4)
            ->replaceStrict(
                [0, 1, 2, 3],
                ['north', 'south', 'east', 'west'],
                returnDtype: 'String',
            )
            ->alias('region'),
        $id->mul(7919)->mod(5000)->alias('customer_id'),
        $id->mul(104729)->mod(100_000)->truediv(100)
            ->alias('amount'),
        $id->mul(31)->mod(7)->eq(0)->alias('returned'),
        $id->cast('String')->str()
            ->replace('^', 'note for order ')
            ->alias('note'),
    )
    ->writeCsv('orders.csv');



use function Phpolars\{col, len, scan_csv};

$query = scan_csv('orders.csv')
    ->filter(
        col('amount')->gt(500)
            ->and(col('returned')->not()),
    )
    ->groupBy('region')
    ->agg(
        len()->alias('orders'),
        col('amount')->mean()->round(2)->alias('mean'),
    )
    ->sort('region');

echo $query->explain(), "\n\n";
echo $query->collect();
SORT BY [col("region")]
  AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
    [len().alias("orders"), col("amount").mean().round().alias("mean")] BY [col("region")]
    FROM
    simple π 2/2 ["region", "amount"]
      Csv SCAN [orders.csv]
      PROJECT 3/6 COLUMNS
      SELECTION: (col("amount") > 500.0) & col("returned").not()
      ESTIMATED ROWS: 1481549

┌────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ region ┆ orders ┆ mean   │
│ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---    │
│ str    ┆ u32    ┆ f64    │
╞════════╪════════╪════════╡
│ east   ┆ 107143 ┆ 750.0  │
│ north  ┆ 107133 ┆ 750.0  │
│ south  ┆ 107142 ┆ 749.99 │
│ west   ┆ 107141 ┆ 750.01 │

PROJECT 3/6 COLUMNS: the reader converts only three columns to values. It still reads and splits every line of the file.
SELECTION: the filter runs during the scan, so rejected rows never reach the aggregation.
ESTIMATED ROWS is the planner’s estimate, not a count.
scan_csv() doesn’t open the file. A missing file raises an error at explain() or collect().
read_csv() would parse all six columns of every row before filtering.
collect(engine: 'streaming') runs the query in batches, which can lower peak memory on large files.

Comparing with py-polars
scripts/pyfixtures.py builds 314 cases with py-polars and writes tests/fixtures/py/expected.json. tests/pyfixtures.php builds the same cases with phpolars and compares column names, data types, and values. Regenerate the fixtures with:

title: Development
text:
Release packaging
The packaging workflow builds the extension inside the official php:8.3-fpm-bookworm, php:8.4-fpm-bookworm, and php:8.5-fpm-bookworm images for x86_64 and arm64. It installs each build with PIE, runs the release checks, and sends requests through PHP-FPM. Each tested php_polars.so is packaged in a zip named as PIE expects, with manifest.json, INSTALL.txt, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt. After a release is published, the release workflow installs each archive into a clean PHP image by hand, and again with pie install, which must pick the prebuilt archive without a Rust toolchain.

PHP build: non-thread-safe (NTS). ZTS builds are not supported.
Operating systems: Linux and macOS. Windows is not supported.

phpolars uses the Polars 0.55.2 Rust crates. The test suite compares it with py-polars 1.43.2, the release whose Rust core is closest to 0.55.2, on a fixed set of cases.

Compared: column names, data types, and values. Floats may differ by a relative tolerance of 1e-9. A case that expects an error must raise the same exception class.
Covered: data frame methods, functions, joins, grouping, windows, sorting, casts, SQL, and the str, dt, list, struct, and arr namespaces.
Not covered: other methods and arguments follow py-polars’ names, but their agreement with py-polars has not been compared.

The verification page lists each case and its result.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Not available

Python callables. py-polars methods that run a Python function per value or per batch, such as map_elements, map_batches, fold, and map_groups, have no equivalent, because PHP code cannot run on Polars threads. DataFrame::mapRows() runs a PHP callable per row on the PHP thread, after collecting.
The GPU engine. collect(engine: 'gpu') throws a ValueError.
Conversion to pandas, NumPy, or PyArrow objects. Data leaves phpolars as PHP values, as files, or through PDO.
Formats left out of a build. Parquet, IPC, JSON, SQL, and table formatting are Cargo features, and an extension built without one raises a ComputeError from that format’s functions. The release binaries include all of them.

title: Coming from py-polars
text: phpolars keeps py-polars’ names and semantics, and most differences come from PHP’s syntax. The test suite compares a fixed set of operations with py-polars 1.43.2, and Compatibility and limitations describes what those cases cover.

Methods are camelCase. Functions are snake_case in the Phpolars namespace. Named parameters are camelCase. PHP has no operator overloading, so arithmetic and comparison are methods: add, sub, mul, truediv, floordiv, mod, pow, eq, ne, gt, ge, lt, le, and, or, not.

title: Coming from py-polars
Coming from py-polars
text:
Values
Results come back as PHP values: int, float, bool, string, null, DateTimeImmutable for dates and datetimes, lists for List columns, and associative arrays for Struct columns. See Types and values.

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Names PHP reserves
PHP keywords cannot be function names, so a few functions take a trailing underscore, as struct_() does: var_(), and the selectors cs\list_(), cs\array_(), cs\empty_(), and cs\enum_(). Methods keep their py names, because PHP allows keywords there: $expr->struct(), $expr->list().

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Python callables
py-polars methods that run a Python function per value or per batch, such as map_elements, map_batches, fold, and map_groups, have no phpolars equivalent. Polars runs expressions on its own threads, and PHP code cannot run there. Use expressions instead. DataFrame::mapRows() is the exception: it runs on the PHP thread, after collecting, and calls a PHP callable per row.

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Small differences

Series::count() keeps py’s meaning (non-null values). Series does not implement Countable; use len().
__toString() gives Polars’ table layout, so echo $df prints like print(df).
DataFrame::toColumns() is a phpolars addition: toDict(asSeries: false).
Strings in arithmetic are literals in phpolars, as they are in comparisons. py treats a string as a column name in some operators (col("a") - "b") but not others (col("a") + "b"); use col('b') for a column.
Series and DataFrame methods never change the object in place. py’s in-place methods (scatter, set, extend, insert_column, replace_column) return a new object.
read_database() takes a PDO connection.

title: Deployment
text:
pie install phpstats/phpolars
PIE resolves the release from Packagist and downloads a prebuilt binary when one matches the PHP version, architecture, and C library. Otherwise it builds the extension from source with the dist profile. It then enables the extension and checks that it loads. A PHP-FPM service, queue workers, and other long-running PHP processes load extensions only when they start, so restart them after installing or upgrading.

title: Deployment

Prebuilt binaries and source builds
Each release attaches prebuilt binaries for:

PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5
NTS builds
Linux on x86_64 and arm64
glibc 2.34 or later (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL 9, or newer)

The binaries are built on Debian Bookworm and do not run on Alpine or other musl systems. macOS, musl Linux, and other platforms build from source. A source build needs a stable Rust toolchain and libclang, and takes several minutes. ZTS (thread-safe) PHP builds are not supported. A build for one PHP minor version loads only in that version, because PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5 have different module APIs.
Each release zip, such as php_php_polars-v0.2.1_php8.4-x86_64-linux-glibc-nts.zip, holds php_polars.so and:

title: Deployment
text:
Ubuntu and Laravel Forge
Forge installs PHP from the ondrej/php PPA, and pie install phpstats/phpolars works there as above. On Ubuntu, PIE enables the extension for both the CLI and PHP-FPM.
To install a binary from the release by hand instead:
sudo cp php_polars.so "$(php -r 'echo ini_get("extension_dir");')/"
echo 'extension=php_polars.so' | sudo tee /etc/php/8.5/mods-available/php_polars.ini
sudo phpenmod -v 8.5 php_polars
sudo systemctl reload php8.5-fpm
When only queue workers, scheduled commands, or Artisan commands use phpolars, enable it for the CLI alone with sudo phpenmod -v 8.5 -s cli php_polars. PHP-FPM workers then never load it, and no FPM reload is needed. After installing or upgrading, restart queue workers, for example with php artisan queue:restart or php artisan horizon:terminate.

title: Deployment
text:
Laravel Herd
A source build, with PIE or by hand, needs phpize and php-config, which Herd’s PHP binaries do not have. Build against Homebrew’s PHP of the same minor version, which has the same module API. For Herd’s PHP 8.5:
git clone https://github.com/phpstats/phpolars && cd phpolars
git checkout v0.2.1
P=$(brew --prefix php@8.5)/bin
PHP=$P/php PHP_CONFIG=$P/php-config LIBCLANG_PATH=$(brew --prefix llvm)/lib cargo build --profile dist
Then add the library to the php.ini that Herd opens from its PHP settings, ~/Library/Application Support/Herd/config/php/85/php.ini, with the path written out in full, and restart Herd:
extension=/path/to/phpolars/target/dist/libphp_polars.dylib
For PHP 8.4, use php@8.4 and config/php/84/php.ini.

title: Deployment
text:
Building from source by hand
git clone https://github.com/phpstats/phpolars && cd phpolars
git checkout v0.2.1
PHP=$(which php) PHP_CONFIG=$(which php-config) cargo build --profile dist
Copy target/dist/libphp_polars.so, or libphp_polars.dylib on macOS, into php-config --extension-dir as php_polars.so, and add extension=php_polars.so to the php.ini that php --ini reports. On macOS with Homebrew, also set LIBCLANG_PATH=$(brew --prefix llvm)/lib. When several PHP versions are installed, point PHP and PHP_CONFIG at the PHP that will load the extension, because the build uses that PHP’s headers.
Build with --profile dist for anything you deploy. The dist profile applies fat LTO, opt-level = "s", and symbol stripping, so its library is much smaller than a release build’s.

Optional formats
The release binaries and a default build include every format. A source build can leave formats out with Cargo features to make the library smaller:







Feature
Provides

Arrow IPC (Feather) reading and writing. It also enables parquet, which Polars 0.55’s IPC reader needs.

title: Deployment
text:
Threads under PHP-FPM
Polars runs queries on a thread pool. FPM workers are separate processes, so each worker that uses phpolars starts its own pool. The INI setting caps the pool per process:
; php.ini
extension=php_polars.so
php_polars.max_threads = 2
The setting defaults to 2 and is PHP_INI_SYSTEM, because the pool starts once per process and cannot be resized. A change takes effect when the process restarts. An explicit POLARS_MAX_THREADS environment variable takes precedence. Phpolars\thread_pool_size() reports the size in effect. Size it so that pm.max_children × max_threads fits the machine’s cores.
PHP closures never run on Polars threads. Every phpolars operation is built from expressions that Polars evaluates natively.

title: Deployment
text:
Memory
Polars allocates with its own allocator, outside PHP’s memory manager. memory_get_usage() and memory_limit do not see that memory, so a process can hold far more than memory_get_peak_usage() reports. Size FPM pools and queue workers by process memory, and limit request data with the application’s own checks. PHP arrays built from a result, for example with rows() or toDicts(), do count against memory_limit. Performance measures memory on large files.

title: Deployment
text:
Checking an installation
The command below checks the CLI:
php -r 'echo phpversion("php_polars"), PHP_EOL;'
PHP-FPM can load a different php.ini, so check it through a web request. tests/deployment.php in the repository runs the same assertions through the CLI and, in scripts/check-fpm and scripts/check-container, through a real FastCGI request:
php tests/deployment.php
docker build --target checks -f docker/Dockerfile -t php-polars-checks .
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t php-polars-runtime .
scripts/check-container php-polars-runtime php-polars-checks

title: Aggregate with expressions
text:
Summarize each group of a DataFrame with several expressions in one agg() call.
Requires the phpolars extension (Getting started). Runnable script: expressions.php.
use Phpolars\DataFrame;
use function Phpolars\{col, len};

$orders = new DataFrame([
    'region' => [
        'north', 'north', 'south', 'south', 'south', 'west',
    ],
    'customer' => ['ana', 'ben', 'ana', 'cy', 'cy', 'di'],
    'amount' => [120.0, 80.0, 45.5, 300.0, 60.0, 95.0],
    'returned' => [false, true, false, false, true, false],
]);

$byRegion = $orders
    ->groupBy('region', maintainOrder: true)
    ->agg(
        len()->alias('orders'),
        col('amount')->sum()->alias('total'),
        col('amount')
            ->filter(col('returned')->not())
            ->sum()
            ->alias('kept'),
        col('customer')->nUnique()->alias('buyers'),
        col('customer')
            ->sortBy('amount', descending: true)
            ->first()
            ->alias('top'),
    );

echo $byRegion;
shape: (3, 6)
┌────────┬────────┬───────┬───────┬────────┬─────┐
│ region ┆ orders ┆ total ┆ kept  ┆ buyers ┆ top │
│ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---    ┆ --- │
│ str    ┆ u32    ┆ f64   ┆ f64   ┆ u32    ┆ str │
╞════════╪════════╪═══════╪═══════╪════════╪═════╡
│ north  ┆ 2      ┆ 200.0 ┆ 120.0 ┆ 2      ┆ ana │
│ south  ┆ 3      ┆ 405.5 ┆ 345.5 ┆ 2      ┆ cy  │
│ west   ┆ 1      ┆ 95.0  ┆ 95.0  ┆ 1      ┆ di  │
└────────┴────────┴───────┴───────┴────────┴─────┘

filter() inside an aggregate limits only that aggregate. kept leaves out returned orders, and orders and total still count them.
sortBy('amount', ...)->first() picks a value by another column’s order. top is the customer with the group’s largest order.
Without maintainOrder: true, the order of the groups can change between runs.

Reference: groupBy() · agg() · Expressions

title: Rolling windows and as-of joins
text:
Give each day of sales the price in force on that date and a mean of units over the last three calendar days, on dates with gaps.
Requires the phpolars extension (Getting started). Runnable script: time-series.php.
use Phpolars\DataFrame;
use function Phpolars\col;

// Daily unit sales, with no rows for March 3 and 7.
$sales = (new DataFrame([
    'date' => [
        '2024-03-01', '2024-03-02', '2024-03-04',
        '2024-03-05', '2024-03-06', '2024-03-08',
    ],
    'units' => [12, 15, 9, 20, 14, 18],
]))->withColumns(col('date')->str()->toDate());

// List prices, each in force until the next change.
$prices = (new DataFrame([
    'from' => ['2024-03-01', '2024-03-05'],
    'price' => [4.50, 4.95],
]))->withColumns(col('from')->str()->toDate());

$priced = $sales
    ->joinAsof($prices, leftOn: 'date', rightOn: 'from')
    ->withColumns(
        col('units')->rollingMeanBy('date', '3d')
            ->round(2)
            ->alias('units_3d'),
    );

echo $priced;
shape: (6, 5)
┌────────────┬───────┬────────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ date       ┆ units ┆ from       ┆ price ┆ units_3d │
│ ---        ┆ ---   ┆ ---        ┆ ---   ┆ ---      │
│ date       ┆ i64   ┆ date       ┆ f64   ┆ f64      │
╞════════════╪═══════╪════════════╪═══════╪══════════╡
│ 2024-03-01 ┆ 12    ┆ 2024-03-01 ┆ 4.5   ┆ 12.0     │
│ 2024-03-02 ┆ 15    ┆ 2024-03-01 ┆ 4.5   ┆ 13.5     │
│ 2024-03-04 ┆ 9     ┆ 2024-03-01 ┆ 4.5   ┆ 12.0     │
│ 2024-03-05 ┆ 20    ┆ 2024-03-05 ┆ 4.95  ┆ 14.5     │
│ 2024-03-06 ┆ 14    ┆ 2024-03-05 ┆ 4.95  ┆ 14.33    │
│ 2024-03-08 ┆ 18    ┆ 2024-03-05 ┆ 4.95  ┆ 16.0     │
└────────────┴───────┴────────────┴───────┴──────────┘

joinAsof() takes the last price whose from is on or before each date.
Both inputs must be sorted by their join columns. Unsorted input raises an InvalidOperationError.
The '3d' window is (date - 3d, date]: it includes the row’s own date and excludes the date three days earlier.
A missing day leaves the window three days long, with fewer rows in it. For March 4, the window holds only March 2 and March 4.
rollingMean(3) would average the last three rows, whatever their dates.

title: phpolars
text:
Query and transform data with Polars from PHP. Use eager data frames, or build lazy queries with expressions.
The Composer package is phpstats/phpolars. PIE installs it as the php_polars extension, which is the name that extension= and phpversion() use. Polars runs inside the PHP process: expressions such as col('units')->mul(col('price')) run on Polars’ own threads, and PHP values are created only when code asks for them, for example with toDicts().
The API follows py-polars, Polars’ Python package, with camelCase method names and snake_case functions. Compatibility and limitations covers the differences and how agreement with py-polars is tested.
The example reads sales.csv, the docs’ example data. Getting started has a complete script and the command that downloads the data.

title: phpolars
text:
What it includes

DataFrame and LazyFrame with py-polars’ methods: select, withColumns, filter, sort, groupBy/agg, join, unique, pivot, unpivot, explode, describe, and more.
Expressions with arithmetic, three-valued logic, aggregations, window functions (over), when/then/otherwise, and the str, dt, list, struct, and name namespaces.
Series, with the same expression methods.
CSV, Parquet, JSON, NDJSON, and Arrow IPC reading and writing, with lazy scans and streaming sinks, and reading and writing through PDO.
SQL queries over data frames.
A thread-pool cap for PHP-FPM (php_polars.max_threads).

title: phpolars
section: The phpolars API or phibble and phplyr
text:
The phpolars API or phibble and phplyr

The phpolars API (Phpolars\DataFrame, LazyFrame, Series, and expressions) follows Polars’ semantics. A missing value is null, and aggregates skip it.
phibble’s Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable runs phibble tables and phplyr pipelines in Polars with dplyr’s semantics, in which null is R’s NA. The adapter belongs to phibble and runs on this extension.

phibble and phplyr covers the choice and the differences in semantics.

title: phibble and phplyr
text: Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable is a phibble table that keeps its data in a Polars DataFrame, so phplyr pipelines that start from it run in Polars. It belongs to phibble (since v0.2.0) and needs the php_polars extension. phibble only suggests the extension, so installing phibble does not install phpolars. phibble’s Backends page compares its table backends.

title: phibble and phplyr
phibble and phplyr
text:
Moving data in and out

PolarsTable::fromPolars($df) wraps a phpolars DataFrame without copying it. A LazyFrame is collected first.
PolarsTable::fromTable($table) copies any phibble table into Polars and keeps types, groups, and factor levels. It throws when a list column would not round-trip exactly, for example when named arrays with different keys would become structs.
$table->polars() returns the underlying phpolars DataFrame.
$table->collect() copies the data into a Phibble\DataFrame.

Without the adapter, Phpolars\DataFrame::fromPhibble($table) reads any phibble table through toColumns(), and $df->toPhibble() returns a Phibble\DataFrame. toPhibble() needs phibble v0.2 or later.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
What runs in Polars
Verbs given column names or phibble expressions (Phibble\Expr, which phplyr’s helpers such as col(), mean(), and n() build) run in Polars with dplyr’s semantics:

NA propagates, and aggregates default to naRm: false.
Grouped mutate() and filter() evaluate aggregates and windows per group.
Groups follow sorted key order.
Joins follow dplyr 1.2, including join_by() inequality and rolling joins.
Pivots and most stringr and lubridate functions also run in Polars.

Some steps cannot run in Polars, and the adapter runs them on a phibble DataFrame and converts the result back:

a verb given a PHP closure, because PHP code cannot run on Polars threads
any verb on a rowwise table
grouped verbs on factor keys that keep empty groups (phibble’s groupBy(drop: false) or phplyr’s group_by(_drop: false)), because Polars does not see empty groups
functions that the translator does not support, such as str_to_title()

PolarsTable::$fallbacks counts these conversions. Set PolarsTable::$strict = true to throw Phibble\Polars\PolarsFallback instead; its message names the verb and the reason. Performance measures the cost of a fallback.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
Missing values
phibble and phplyr treat PHP null as R’s NA, and a pipeline on a PolarsTable keeps those semantics. The phpolars API itself (DataFrame, LazyFrame, Expr, and Series) follows Polars, which treats null differently. Code moved from a phplyr pipeline to direct phpolars calls can return different results on the same data.








Operation
phplyr, as in dplyr
phpolars, as in Polars




sum, mean, min, max, std
NA if any value is NA, unless naRm: true
Nulls are skipped. col('x')->sum() over [1, null, 3] is 4.


Counting
n() counts rows
count() counts non-null values; len() counts rows


Comparison with null
NA
null. eqMissing() and neMissing() treat null as a value.


Arithmetic with null
NA
null


filter
A row whose condition is NA is dropped
A row whose condition is null is dropped


Sorting
NA sorts last
null sorts first; pass nullsLast: true


Join keys
NA matches NA unless naMatches: 'never'
null matches nothing unless nullsEqual: true


NaN
is.na() is true for NaN
NaN is a float value. isNull() is false for it; use isNan().



To get dplyr’s results from phpolars, compare nullCount() with zero before aggregating, sort with nullsLast: true, and join with nullsEqual: true.

title: Expressions
text:
An Expr describes a computation on columns. Expressions are built with col(), lit(), when(), and the other functions below, and are evaluated by verbs such as select(), withColumns(), filter(), and agg(). They never hold PHP closures, so Polars runs them on its own threads.
Operands of comparison and arithmetic methods may be an Expr or a PHP value. PHP strings there are string literals.

title: Expressions
text:
Missing values
Expressions follow Polars’ null semantics. Arithmetic and comparisons with null give null. Aggregations such as sum(), mean(), min(), and max() skip nulls, count() counts non-null values, and len() counts rows. filter() drops rows whose condition is null. isNull(), fillNull(), dropNulls(), eqMissing(), and neMissing() handle nulls explicitly. NaN is a float value, so isNull() is false for it and isNan() is true. phibble and phplyr compares these rules with dplyr’s.

title: Expressions
text:
Windows and order
over() evaluates an expression within groups and maps the result back to every row. orderBy sets the order for order-dependent expressions such as cumSum() and shift().

    'date',
    'product',
    'units',
    col('units')->sum()->over('product')->alias('product_total'),
    col('units')->cumSum()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('running'),
    col('units')->shift()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('previous'),
    col('units')->rank('dense', descending: true)->alias('rank'),
);
